description: "Dyadic dependent terms, why the triangle term breaks, and how to tell whether your model actually fits."
date: 2026-08-09

[Part 1](../2026-08-09-ergm-interpretation_part1/index.qmd) built up an ERGM using terms
that assume ties form independently of one another. That assumption made the
models easy to fit and easy to interpret, but it was not a great model. We saw that the actual observed advice network had more reciprocated ties and more triangles than an independence model could produce.

This post takes up the dyadic dependent terms that can represent those patterns, discusses some challenges with estimation when those terms are in our model, and explores how to check whether a fitted model is any good.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(statnet)

load("par5.RData")
load("par.friends.RData")
```
:::


## Dependence among ties

As soon as our theory indicates that whether $i$ sends a tie to $j$ depends on the other ties in the network, our model requires dyadic dependent terms and this moves us away from logistic regression. Two teachers may be more likely to exchange advice because they already share a partner, or because advice tends to be reciprocated. Those are statements about ties conditioning on other ties in the network.

The classic way to capture clustering was a simple `triangle` term, counting the triangles a tie would close. A positive coefficient would say triangles appear more often than chance would produce. This makes intuitive sense, but, as we will see, it often resulted in degenerate models. 

The current alternative to 'triangle' is the geometrically weighted edgewise shared partner statistic, `gwesp`. Rather than counting each additional shared partner equally, it discounts them: going from zero shared partners to one matters a great deal, from five to six much less. That diminishing return is both substantively sensible and far better behaved during estimation.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod6 <- ergm(par5 ~ edges + mutual + edgecov(par.friends) +
               nodeicov("COMP.1") + nodeocov("COMP.1") +
               twopath + gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE))
```

The decay parameter — `0.25` here — controls how quickly additional shared
partners are discounted. Setting `fixed = TRUE` treats it as known rather than
estimating it, which is the common practice though you can also allow for it to be estimated as well.  For more information see [Hunter and Handcock (2006)](https://www.jstor.org/stable/27594198) as well as [Hunter (2007)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378873306000396?via%3Dihub)

## A full model

Let's build a full model here. This is the full specification from the published
analysis (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/puar.12362): structural terms for reciprocity, twopaths, edgewise and dyadwise shared partners, and in- and out-degree distributions, alongside the attribute and friendship effects from Part 1.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
final <- ergm(par5 ~ edges + mutual + twopath +
                gwesp(0.693, fixed = TRUE) + gwdsp(0.693, fixed = TRUE) +
                edgecov(par.friends) +
                gwidegree(0.693, fixed = TRUE) + gwodegree(0.693, fixed = TRUE) +
                nodematch("GRADE") + absdiff("YRSDIST") +
                nodeicov("YRSDIST") + nodeocov("YRSDIST") +
                nodeifactor("EDUC") + nodeofactor("EDUC") +
                nodeicov("EFFIC") + nodeocov("EFFIC") +
                nodeicov("COMP.1") + nodeocov("COMP.1"))
```

The `gwidegree` and `gwodegree` terms deserve a word of caution, because the direction of the relationship has often been misinterpreted. A negative coefficient indicates *centralization* — degree concentrated among fewer actors — rather than the
opposite. Reading these the wrong way is a common error. Here is a great explainer by [Levy and colleagues](https://figshare.com/articles/poster/Interpretation_of_GW-Degree_Estimates_in_ERGMs/3465020?file=5454032) along with a link to an awesome shiny app to see this in action.

## Degeneracy

Let's move on to what happens when our model fails to converge and thus is degenerate. Model degeneracy means the fitted parameters imply a distribution that places nearly all its probability on networks that look nothing like the one we observed. 

As noted above, the `triangle` term is a well known problem in models and leads to degeneracy. We will use a simulated high
school friendship network that comes with the `statnet` package for demonstration purposes.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data("faux.magnolia.high")
magnolia <- faux.magnolia.high
plot(magnolia, vertex.cex = 0.75)
```

In both plots, the simulated network statistics for edges and triangles climbs, and keeps climbing, toward networks far denser than anything in the data. A model whose simulated

### Why the triangle term does this

Let's try to understand more about why this occurs and why the geometrically weighted terms provide a solution. 

With a positive coefficient on the `triangle` term , every tie that closes a triangle makes additional triangles more likely, which makes additional ties more likely, which closes more triangles. The statistic feeds back on itself with nothing to dampen it. Adding the hundredth shared partner counts exactly as much as adding the first, so the model has no way to express "clustering is good, but in moderation."

### The fix

The fix is a term for capturing the diminishing marginal returns of additional triadic closure.

Thus, we replace `triangle` with `gwesp`, whose geometric discounting means each additional shared partner contributes less than the one before. This is precisely the dampening the raw triangle count lacked. In addition, let's also add several attribute terms that also help account for clustering in the network. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit2 <- ergm(magnolia ~ edges + gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE) +
               nodematch("Grade") + nodematch("Race") + nodematch("Sex"),
             control = control.ergm(seed = 1,
                                    MCMC.samplesize = 50000,
                                    MCMC.interval = 1000))
```

The plots on the left are known as trace plots. Each shows the difference between the simulated and observed value of a statistic as the chain progresses. What you want is a stationary band with values bouncing around zero with no trend. The density plots on the right should be roughly symmetric and centered at zero, indicating that simulated networks resemble the
observed one on each statistic.

Compare these with the runaway chains we saw above. There the statistics moved quickly away from the observed values and never returned. Here they bounce around them randomly and are always centered on the true value.

This model takes a few minutes to run. Depending on your network's size and model complexity, some ERGM specifications run for hours or long. Starting a model before bed and hoping to find a converged one in the morning is a reasonable routine.

### A point to remember

Notice what actually changed between the model that failed and the model that
worked. Students form friendships with others in the same grade, of the same
race, of the same sex, and those homophilous ties produce triangles as a
byproduct. In our failed model, we asked the triangle term to explain all of that clustering on its own, and so it kept wanting to build more and more triangles and resulted in a degenerate model. Thus you need to think carefully about the processes at work in your network and use the ergm terms that capture those processes in your model.

Degeneracy usually looks like a computational problem but it is mostly about a poor model specification. As always, theory needs to come first.

## Goodness of fit

Simply getting a model to converge does not mean we have a good model fit. A model can converge cleanly and still fail to reproduce
different features of the network. In general, we ask two questions about our model to understand its fit.

First, does the model reproduce the statistics it was fit on? This is mostly about degeneracy and convergence.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gof(mod6, GOF = ~ model)
```

Second, does it reproduce features it was *not* fit on? Here we are looking to see if our model simulates networks that have similar macro properties to our observed network. It is important to note here, that no term in our model ensures that we capture these macro properties. Rather, they are built up from the small, local terms we put in our model.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(gof(mod6))

In each panel the observed network is the solid line and the simulated distribution is the boxplots. You want the observed line sitting inside the bulk of the simulated range. Where it strays outside, the model is missing something.

You can also name your own statistic, like the triad census, and a model reproducing the full census is capturing local structure well:
